_note: Depiction rules for generated featured images, as patterns rather than prose, because prose in a README is advisory and one session away from gone. Read by imagepolicy.mjs and enforced twice: on the generation BRIEF (geminibrowser.mjs, before a shot is worth making) and on the shipped ALT text (makefeatured.mjs, which every image must pass). Case-insensitive. `refuse` aborts; `warn` prints and continues.
_structure: Every brand gets the `shared` profile plus the one named in `brands`. A brand missing from that map falls back to `shared` alone. A rule is {pattern, why} and may add `unless`: a second pattern that, when it matches, skips the rule - used where a ban has a legitimate context, such as a body part appearing in a radiograph.

shared._why: True of any brand here: a synthetic person must not be passed off as a real one, and a brand's trade dress must not imply the client dispenses or endorses it.

refuse.pattern: (our|a real|an actual|real) patient|patient (of|at) (the|this|our) clinic|\bour provider\b|\bour staff\b|\bour (doctor|nurse|physician)s?\b
refuse.why: these people are illustrations; presenting one as a patient, provider or staff member is a fabricated record
a before/after pair promises an outcome, which is an implied-outcome claim on a YMYL medical page
recognizable trade dress on the client's own graphic implies they dispense or endorse that brand - use an unbranded device and the generic name in copy
graphic injury is fear marketing and it is what makes a medical page unshareable (a blood pressure monitor or reading is a measurement, not an injury, so "blood pressure" is exempt)

wellness._why: irvingwellnessclinic. A person is often the right subject here - the posts are about elective care someone chooses. The bans are the documented weight-stigma tropes (the Rudd Center published a free image bank precisely because media kept using them). A larger-bodied subject on weight-loss content is CORRECT; the harm is in showing that body differently from every other portrait in the set. See section 24 of the irvingwellnessclinic-design skill.

refuse.why: a body with the face removed is the most common and most dehumanizing weight-stigma trope - show a person, face visible
isolating a body part turns a person into the thing being judged
shames the 'before' and promises an outcome

refuse.pattern: bathroom scale|weighing scale|(standing|stepping|steps) on a scale|(tape measure|measuring tape)|waist measurement
refuse.why: staging the measurement is what makes weight-loss imagery punitive; the copy may name the scale, the picture must not stage it
a subject performing failure - the article is about a drug plateau, not a personal one
optics chosen to make the body look larger than it is
undress and unflattering clothing are stigma cues; ordinary well-fitting clothes are the parity test
this clinic's provider is an APRN - depicting or naming a doctor misstates the credential

warn.why: food-as-blame prop; fine on a nutrition explainer, a stigma cue beside a person
sedentary framing implies the stall is a character failure
clinical or blunt body language in a visual brief pushes the model toward caricature - describe the body plainly instead

er._why: erofirving / eroflufkin / erofwhiterock. NO PEOPLE AT ALL, which is the opposite of the wellness profile and follows from what these posts are. An ER post is a triage decision - 'is this chest pain the ER?' - so a person in the frame is either a patient who does not exist or a clinician who does not work there, and both ER skills say real facility and real staff only (White Rock's provider bylines are blocked outright for want of consent). A reader arriving mid-panic should feel held, not sold to. That leaves two honest options, and they cover every post: the `type` layout, or an object still life. Verified 2026-09-08: the stock service images already on erofwhiterock (a smiling nurse at a CT scanner, red-glow pain overlays) are exactly what these rules exclude, so site media is not a way around this.

refuse.why: no people on the ER brands: a depicted patient does not exist and a depicted clinician does not work there. Use the `type` layout or an object still life
distress staging is fear marketing; the ER voice is calm and clinical
implies this ER runs emergency transport, which it does not, and stages urgency the copy is not allowed to claim

refuse.pattern: \bno wait\b|short(er)? wait|\bminutes? wait\b|wait time|faster than|\bhospital (ed|er)\b|vs\.? hospital|beat the (wait|hospital)
refuse.why: anti-pattern in all three ER skills: door-to-provider claims are self-anchored and live in copy, never in a graphic, and comparing against hospital EDs damages the referral relationships this ER depends on
a person's body part still implies a patient, and the object photographs alone just as well

a body part with no owner named is still a person in the frame. `face` and `skin` are deliberately NOT in this rule: "lying face up", "the hands of a clock" and a snake's "skin" are photographic or animal idiom, and refusing those cost two false refusals of legitimate object briefs on 2026-09-08. `unless` exempts medical imaging: a radiograph of a forearm is a picture of bones, not a person in the frame

warn.why: 'call 911' belongs in copy as a disclaimer; as an image it is fear staging
these are freestanding ERs, not hospitals - check the picture does not imply inpatient care they do not provide
body-part word in an ER brief - harmless in photographic phrasing, but check the picture implies no person
